name: Cheerleader effect
statement: The same face is rated as more attractive when seen in a group than when seen alone, by about one and a half to two and a half points on a hundred-point scale.
meaning: The claim is narrow. A rater sees one photograph of a person alone and another of the same person flanked by others, and gives an attractiveness rating for the target both times. The rating in the group condition comes out slightly higher. Everything about the comparison is within-subject and within-face, so the effect is a shift in a judgement about one individual, not a claim that groups are attractive. Walker and Vul's abstract explains it by ensemble coding. The visual system computes an ensemble representation of faces presented in a group, individual members are biased towards that average, and average faces are attractive. That is the hierarchical encoding of their title. The name is borrowed from a line in the sitcom How I Met Your Mother, in the 2008 episode 'Not a Father's Day' written by Robia Rashid and directed by Pamela Fryman, as Ojiro and colleagues record.

origin.note: 'Hierarchical encoding makes individuals in a group seem more attractive' ran online on 25 October 2013 and in the January 2014 issue. Its abstract reports five experiments in which subjects rated faces presented either alone or in a group of the same gender. The article is closed access and was not read for this entry. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record no repository copy, Vul's laboratory publication page returned a server error, and the Internet Archive was offline on the day of checking. Its abstract, the publisher's own press release and later papers that describe or replicate it are the sources for everything said about it here.

evidence: The Association for Psychological Science's release on the paper says five experiments used over 130 undergraduates rating pictures of 100 people. Sometimes the target sat in a group portrait with two other people, and sometimes the picture was cropped to show the person alone. Other experiments used collages of 4, 9 and 16 pictures. The release puts the benefit at enough to move someone from the 49th to the 51st percentile of attractiveness, and quotes Vul saying the effect is definitely small. Experiment 4 is the one later work has chased. Ojiro and colleagues describe it as 37 undergraduates at the University of California, San Diego, 13 men and 24 women, rating targets surrounded by 0 to 16 other faces, with ratings higher whenever any surrounding face was present and no effect of how many there were. They give its partial eta squared as .197. Those figures are read off Ojiro and colleagues, not off Walker and Vul. The best-measured version of the effect comes from Flinders University. Carragher, Lawrence, Thomas and Nicholls recruited 64 and then 66 participants and analysed 50 and 60, after excluding left- and mixed-handers and a few outliers. Ratings ran along a visual analogue scale from 'Very Unattractive' at 0% to 'Very Attractive' at 100%. All six of their group conditions were reliable, with Cohen's d from 0.46 to 0.67 and 95% intervals on the gain running from [0.49, 2.09] to [1.32, 3.00] percentage points. They summarise the effect as an increase within the range of 1.5 to 2%. Carragher, Thomas, Gwinn and Nicholls analysed 28, 31, 31 and 29 participants across three experiments and found the same band, for example 1.64% with d = 0.71 and a 95% interval of [0.79, 2.48] percentage points. Kramer, Javorková and Jones put the gain at 2.54% and 2.10% in two Bayesian experiments of 71 and 70 people.

replication.headline: Faces gain roughly 1.5 to 2.5 points on a hundred-point scale in a group, in laboratory after laboratory, while the group-size manipulation of the original's fourth experiment failed twice in Japanese samples.
replication.detail: Carragher, Lawrence, Thomas and Nicholls call theirs the first replication of Walker and Vul, using internet-collected photographs and Experiment 4's presentation timing. Faces were more attractive in every group arrangement they tried, and the spatial layout made no difference: a Bayesian ANOVA put the data 8.96 times more likely under the null for the position of the distractors, and 4.41 times for the position of the target. Against this sit two replications by Ojiro, Gobara, Nam, Sasaki, Kishimoto, Yamada and Miura, run online with Japanese participants. The first used Walker and Vul's own stimuli, supplied by the authors, with 95 participants, and gave F(2.32, 218.01) = 0.128, p = .91, partial eta squared .001. The second used 300 Japanese faces collected from the web with 153 participants and gave F(2.66, 404.55) = 2.587, p = .060, partial eta squared .017. Both samples were larger than the original, 2.5 and 4.1 times over. Neither main effect of group size reached significance. The authors read the second as tracing the original's pattern, and suggest that matching the race of the faces to that of the observers may matter, a proposal they did not test against a contrasting condition. Elsewhere the effect keeps appearing. Carragher, Thomas and Nicholls report that they reliably replicated it across three further experiments. Hattori, Watanabe and Suzuki replicated it with groups of similarly attractive faces and found it largest when women rated male faces. Kramer, Javorková and Jones found it for familiar and unfamiliar faces alike, with an interaction estimate of zero and a 95% credible interval of [−0.03, 0.03]. Wang and colleagues tested 473 subjects across five experiments, some of them preregistered, and found the size of the effect changes with the time a group is shown before the target is cued and not with the time after. Peng, Mao, Pagliaro, Roberts and Livi confirmed it in 813 Chinese participants on a ten-point scale.

study.cite: Carragher, D. J., Lawrence, B. J., Thomas, N. A., & Nicholls, M. E. R. (2018). Visuospatial asymmetries do not modulate the cheerleader effect. Scientific Reports, 8, 2548.

replicated.weighting: Experiment 1, left-visual-field distractor condition, 50 analysed of 64 recruited

limits: The mechanism in the title is the part that has weakened. Carragher, Thomas, Gwinn and Nicholls built morph faces by digitally averaging each group of three. Every morph beat the three faces it was made from, by 16.57% on average. If hierarchical encoding drove the effect, a target far below its group's morph should gain the most. The correlation between the two measures was r(30) = 0.110, 95% interval [−0.261, 0.452], p = .564. Faces still gained 0.75% when the flanking images were houses rather than faces, and houses gained 1.17% in groups of houses. The authors put the gain at about 1.5% where an ensemble average with facial characteristics could form and about 0.8% where it could not, and conclude that hierarchical encoding makes at most a minimal contribution. They also read the gap between those two figures as partial support for it, which is not the same as a refutation. Carragher and colleagues record two results Walker and Vul had flagged as awkward for their own account: adding faces did not enlarge the effect, and blurring the faces did not either. Ying, Burns, Lin and Xu report no boost at all when every face in the scene is identical, where Carragher and colleagues found a reduced but reliable gain there, d = 0.60. Hsieh, Gwinn, Brooks, Stephen, Carragher and Nicholls found the effect only when raters judged images after they had been removed from the screen, and not when the images stayed visible, which makes it a memory bias rather than a perceptual one. It was larger for bodies than for faces. Who gains is unsettled. Messner, Carnelli and Höhener tested 586 of 605 people on Amazon Mechanical Turk who each rated a face only once, and analysed across 24 face sets rather than across participants. Low-attractiveness targets rose from 39.10 alone to 45.48 among equally unattractive flankers, and fell to 36.25 among attractive ones. High-attractiveness targets rose from 58.44 to 62.06 among unattractive flankers and did not move among attractive ones, 58.85, p = .54. Burns, Yang and Ying report the same reversal and say less attractive targets gain more. Carragher, Thomas and Nicholls found the size of the effect unrelated to the target's own attractiveness, to the group's, or to the group's averaged face. McDowell and Starratt report a conceptual replication for female attractiveness and for value as a romantic partner, and only when the group held some highly attractive members and the target cleared a minimum of its own. No meta-analysis of the cheerleader effect was located, and no multi-laboratory registered replication of it was located either. The search covered Crossref, DataCite, PubMed, Europe PMC, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, OSF and the open web on 17 August 2026. Almost all of this work is laboratory or online rating of photographs by young adults, and none of it follows anyone into a bar.
misreadings: The unit is the trap. An increase of two points is two points on a scale from 0 to 100, not a 2% gain on the rating a face already had, and Walker and Vul's own gloss was a move from the 49th to the 51st percentile. Nothing in the literature supports the advice the name attracts. The effect is not about cheerleaders, or about attractive company: Ojiro and colleagues trace the phrase to a 2008 episode of How I Met Your Mother, Carragher and colleagues got a cheerleader effect out of photographs of houses, and Messner and colleagues found the largest gains beside unattractive flankers. The second confusion is with a different finding. Van Osch, Blanken, Meijs and van Wolferen's group attractiveness effect is the gap between how attractive a group looks as a whole and the mean of its members rated one at a time. Their abstract puts it at Cohen's d = 0.60 across 33 comparisons in nine studies, medium to large, and moderated by group size, while the cheerleader effect in Walker and Vul's Experiment 4 was not. The two are routinely quoted as one number. Van Osch and Sleegers later tested 621 people and found the group attractiveness effect reverses for relatively unattractive groups, which is a result about groups and says nothing about individuals within them.

sources.text: Walker, D., & Vul, E. (2014). Hierarchical encoding makes individuals in a group seem more attractive. Psychological Science, 25(1), 230-235. The founding paper. Closed access: on 17 August 2026 Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all reported no open copy anywhere, a CORE search returned nothing, Vul's laboratory publication page at evullab.org returned HTTP 500 and the Internet Archive was offline. Only the abstract at Crossref was read, and the paper's design and figures are quoted here from Ojiro and colleagues (2015), Carragher and colleagues (2018, 2019) and the publisher's press release.

Association for Psychological Science (2013). People seem more attractive in a group than they do apart. The publisher's release on Walker and Vul, dated 29 October 2013. Source for the count of over 130 undergraduates across five experiments, the pictures of 100 people, the group portrait with two other people, the collages of 4, 9 and 16 pictures, the 49th to 51st percentile figure and Vul's remark that the effect is small.

Ojiro, Y., Gobara, A., Nam, G., Sasaki, K., Kishimoto, R., Yamada, Y., & Miura, K. (2015). Two replications of 'Hierarchical encoding makes individuals in a group seem more attractive (2014; Experiment 4)'. The Quantitative Methods for Psychology, 11(2), r8-r11. Read in full from the journal's PDF. Source for both replications of the group-size manipulation, for the description of Walker and Vul's Experiment 4, for its partial eta squared of .197, for the suggestion about matching the race of faces and observers, and for the sitcom origin of the name.

Carragher, D. J., Lawrence, B. J., Thomas, N. A., & Nicholls, M. E. R. (2018). Visuospatial asymmetries do not modulate the cheerleader effect. Scientific Reports, 8, 2548. Read in full from the PubMed Central JATS XML and again from the publisher's page. Source for the first replication, the recruited and analysed sample sizes, the six condition-level 95% intervals, the Cohen's d values and the two Bayes factors.

Carragher, D. J., Thomas, N. A., Gwinn, O. S., & Nicholls, M. E. R. (2019). Limited evidence of hierarchical encoding in the cheerleader effect. Scientific Reports, 9, 9329. Read in full from the PubMed Central JATS XML. Source for the morph-face results, the r = 0.110 correlation, the identical-distractor and house conditions, the sample sizes and the authors' own reading of their findings as partial support for hierarchical encoding.

Carragher, D. J., Thomas, N. A., Gwinn, O. S., & Nicholls, M. E. R. (2020). The cheerleader effect is robust to experimental manipulations of presentation time. Journal of Cognitive Psychology, 32(5-6), 553-561. Closed at the publisher, and the accepted manuscript deposited at the University of Stirling returned HTTP 403 to every request on 17 August 2026. The PsyArXiv preprint of the same title is cited beside it and its abstract was read there.

Carragher, D. J., Thomas, N. A., Gwinn, O. S., & Nicholls, M. E. R. (2019). The cheerleader effect is robust to experimental manipulations of presentation time. PsyArXiv preprint. Abstract read at the OSF API: group images were shown for 300, 1000, 2000, 3000 or 7000 milliseconds before the target was cued, faces were more attractive in every group condition, and uncued presentation time did not modulate the size of the increase.

Carragher, D. J., Thomas, N. A., & Nicholls, M. E. R. (2021). The dissociable influence of social context on judgements of facial attractiveness and trustworthiness. British Journal of Psychology, 112(4), 902-933. Closed access; the abstract was read at PubMed. Source for the three further replications and for the size of the effect being unrelated to the target's attractiveness, the group's, or the group's averaged face.

Ying, H., Burns, E., Lin, X., & Xu, H. (2019). Ensemble statistics shape face adaptation and the cheerleader effect. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 148(3), 421-436. Closed access; the abstract was read at PubMed. Source for the report that no boost occurs when every face in the scene is identical.

Burns, E. J., Yang, W., & Ying, H. (2021). Friend effects framework: Contrastive and hierarchical processing in cheerleader effects. Cognition, 212, 104715. Closed access; the abstract was read at PubMed. Source for the reverse cheerleader effect beside highly attractive faces and for less attractive targets gaining more.

Hsieh, J. Y. J., Gwinn, O. S., Brooks, K. R., Stephen, I. D., Carragher, D. J., & Nicholls, M. E. R. (2021). The 'cheerleader effect' in facial and bodily attractiveness: A result of memory bias and not perceptual encoding. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 74(5), 972-980. Closed access; the abstract was read at Crossref and again at PubMed. Source for the split between memory and perception and for the effect being larger for bodies.

Messner, C., Carnelli, M., & Höhener, P. S. (2021). Change in evaluation mode can cause a cheerleader effect. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 607448. Read in full from the PubMed Central JATS XML. Source for the 605 participants completed and 586 analysed, for the condition means at each level of target and flanker attractiveness, and for the analysis being run across 24 face sets.

McDowell, J., & Starratt, V. G. (2019). Experimental examination and extension of the cheerleader effect. Personality and Individual Differences, 147, 245-249. Closed at the publisher; the abstract was read at the Nova Southeastern University repository, which holds no full text. Source for the conceptual replication and for the moderators of target sex, baseline attractiveness, group composition and the trait being rated.

Peng, C., Mao, Y., Pagliaro, S., Roberts, S., & Livi, S. (2020). Are individuals perceived as more attractive within a group? A confirmative study of group attractiveness effect and the cheerleader effect in China. Healthcare, 8(3), 344. Read in full from the PubMed Central JATS XML. Source for the 813 participants of Study I, in which the cheerleader effect was tested; the 1,005 of the abstract adds the 192 retained in Study II, which tested only the group attractiveness effect.

Hattori, Y., Watanabe, N., & Suzuki, A. (2019). The cheerleader effect for a group of similarly attractive faces: Modulation by the observer and face gender. The Japanese Journal of Psychonomic Science, 38(1), 13-25. Free access at J-Stage and the PDF was downloaded, but the body is in Japanese, so only the English abstract was used: the source for the replication with similarly attractive groups and for the effect being largest when women rated male faces. Its DOI, 10.14947/psychono.38.6, resolves at neither Crossref nor DataCite, so the article page is cited instead.

Kramer, R. S. S., Javorková, N., & Jones, A. L. (2024). No influence of face familiarity on the cheerleader effect. Visual Cognition, 32(3), 181-191. Read in full from the author-deposited PDF at Figshare. Source for the null interaction with familiarity, its credible interval, and the gains of 2.54% and 2.10% in samples of 71 and 70.

van Osch, Y., Blanken, I., Meijs, M. H. J., & van Wolferen, J. (2015). A group's physical attractiveness is greater than the average attractiveness of its members. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 41(4), 559-574. Closed at the publisher; the only open deposit is a data archive at DataverseNL with no manuscript in it, so the abstract at the Tilburg University research portal is what was read. The group attractiveness effect, and the source for d = 0.60 across 33 comparisons in nine studies. Messner and colleagues cite this paper as one that failed to replicate the cheerleader effect, which could not be checked against the paper itself.

van Osch, Y., & Sleegers, W. W. A. (2021). Replicating and reversing the group attractiveness effect: Relatively unattractive groups are perceived as less attractive than the average attractiveness of their members. Acta Psychologica, 217, 103331. Abstract read at PubMed; the source for N = 621 and for the reversal, which is about groups rather than individuals.

Wang, S., Ying, H., Wang, Q., Li, L., Lei, X., Krueger, F., & Han, C. (2025). Timing is everything: Unraveling the temporal dynamics of the cheerleader effect. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 119, 104758. The published article is closed; the preprint abstract was read at the OSF API. Five experiments, in laboratory and online and partly preregistered, on 473 subjects, reporting that pre-cue time changes the size of the effect and post-cue time does not.

Zheng, R., & Zhou, G. (2022). My group is more important than yours in the cheerleader effect of facial attractiveness perception. Journal of Vision, 22(14), 3405. A conference abstract, the nearest thing located to a test of whether the effect differs for own-group and other-group faces. Metadata verified at Crossref; the publisher's page returned HTTP 403, the text was not obtained, and no claim here comes from it.

Zhou, Y., & Kawabata, H. (2022). You and your cats appear more attractive in a crowd of cats: The cheerleader effect in human/animal facial attractiveness. Current Psychology, 42(33), 29499-29509. Located, metadata verified at Crossref, closed with no abstract obtainable, not read; no claim here comes from it.
Carragher, D. J. (2022). Examining the cheerleader effect. Nature Reviews Psychology, 1(6), 316. Located, metadata verified at Crossref, not read; no claim here comes from it.
